hints: Look at Fig. 5.1 for a functional group that contains both C=O and a C-N link and think about which groups are hydrolysed by hot aqueous acid.
walkthrough:
Spot the weak link in acid**
Picture what stomach acid does. It does not break strong $\text{C-C}$ bonds or benzene rings. It breaks bonds formed by condensation, especially amides and esters, by adding water back across them. Scan atorvastatin and you will find one amide link, $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$, joining the central pyrrole part to the phenylamino group.
Final answer: Draw a line through the amide C-N bond, the bond between the $\text{C=O}$ carbon and the $\text{NH}$ nitrogen on the left side of the molecule.

hints: Scan the right hand side chain for O-H and N-H bonds and recall what type of intermolecular attraction these groups can make with water molecules.
walkthrough:
Link structure to dissolving**
Dissolving means swapping attractions. For a big organic molecule to dissolve, part of it must attract water strongly. Look at the side chain: two alcohol $\text{-OH}$ groups, one carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ group, plus an amide $\text{-CONH-}$ group. All contain H attached to O or N, and lone pairs on O or N.

Name the attraction**
Those $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{N-H}$ groups can donate hydrogen bonds to water, and the lone pairs on the O atoms can accept hydrogen bonds from water. These solute to water hydrogen bonds release enough energy to help pull the molecule into solution, even though much of the molecule is hydrophobic.
Final answer: Atorvastatin contains $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NH}$ groups / polar $\text{C=O}$ O atoms which can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

hints: Count carbons carefully from the three benzene rings, the central pyrrole ring, the isopropyl group and the side chain, remembering each unlabelled corner is a carbon.
walkthrough:
Count systematically**
Work round the diagram and count each element. The three phenyl rings give $6 + 6 + 6 = 18$ carbons, the central five membered pyrrole ring gives 4 carbons plus 1 nitrogen, the isopropyl group gives 3 carbons, the amide $\text{C=O}$ gives 1 carbon, and the long acid side chain gives 7 carbons. Total $33$ carbons, with $2$ nitrogens, $5$ oxygens and $1$ fluorine. With H given as $35$, the formula is $\text{C}_{33}\text{H}_{35}\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{5}\text{F}$.

hints: Focus on the saturated side chain and look for a carbon attached to four different groups, especially carbons bearing OH.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
A chiral carbon has four different atoms or groups attached. Benzene carbons, $\text{C=O}$ carbons and $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons cannot be chiral. Move along the side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_{2}\text{-COOH}$. Each $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbon is bonded to H, OH, and two different carbon chain segments left and right, so each is chiral. There are exactly two of them.
Final answer: Circle the two $\text{CH(OH)}$ carbon atoms in the dihydroxy acid side chain, the carbons bearing the two $\text{OH}$ groups.

hints: Think about how a drug fits into a protein binding site in the body and whether mirror image shapes fit equally well.
walkthrough:
Think about shape and receptors**
Enzymes and receptors are made from chiral amino acids, so their binding pockets are chiral. One optical isomer of atorvastatin has the correct 3D shape to fit and block cholesterol synthesis effectively. The mirror image fits poorly, so it is less active and could cause side effects, therefore a single isomer is prepared.
Final answer: Only one optical isomer has the required / better biological activity, the other isomer may be inactive or have unwanted effects.

hints: Use Table 5.1 to list which proton types appear above $\delta$ 6.5, then count those protons on the three aromatic rings plus the amide NH and acid OH in Fig. 5.1.
walkthrough:
Pick out who resonates that far downfield**
From Table 5.1, in $\delta = 6.5$ to $13.0$ ppm you find H attached to aromatic ring ($6.0$ to $9.0$), amide $\text{RCONHR}$ ($5.0$ to $12.0$) and carboxylic acid $\text{RCOOH}$ ($9.0$ to $13.0$). Now count in atorvastatin: phenyl ring $5$ H + phenyl ring $5$ H + 4-fluorophenyl ring $4$ H $= 14$ aromatic H, plus $1$ amide $\text{NH}$ plus $1$ carboxylic acid $\text{OH}$ $= 16$ H in total.

hints: Recall which protons in $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NH}$ groups disappear from a proton NMR spectrum when the sample is shaken with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$.
Count all such exchangeable protons in atorvastatin from its two alcohol groups, its carboxylic acid group and its amide group.
walkthrough:
Identify the disappearing protons**
Protons on O or N are labile. In $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$, the reaction $\text{R-OH} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-OD} + \text{HOD}$ replaces H by D. Deuterium does not resonate in the proton NMR region, so that peak vanishes.

Count them in atorvastatin**
Atorvastatin has two alcohol $\text{OH}$ protons + one carboxylic acid $\text{OH}$ proton + one amide $\text{NH}$ proton $= 4$ exchangeable protons. All four exchange with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$, so 4 hydrogens would not show a peak.
Final answer: 4 protons do not show a peak.\nThe $\text{NH}$ / $\text{OH}$ protons exchange with D from $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ to form $\text{ND}$ / $\text{OD}$ which give no proton NMR signal.

hints: Recall that $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ is a strong reducing agent that reduces carbonyls in acids and amides but leaves isolated C=C, aromatic rings and alcohols unchanged.
Think about what carbonyl containing group becomes a $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ group and what $\text{-CONH-}$ group becomes a $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{NH-}$ group on reduction.
walkthrough:
Select the reducible groups**
$\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ delivers hydride to highly polar $\text{C=O}$ groups. In atorvastatin the carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ and the amide $\text{-CONH-}$ are reduced. Alcohols, aromatic rings, C-F and the pyrrole ring are not reduced under these conditions.

Name the products**
Reduction of a carboxylic acid gives a primary alcohol: $\text{RCOOH} \rightarrow \text{RCH}_{2}\text{OH}$. Reduction of an amide removes the carbonyl oxygen to give an amine: $\text{RCONHR'} \rightarrow \text{RCH}_{2}\text{NHR'}$. So the new groups are a primary alcohol from the acid and an amine from the amide.
Final answer: Functional groups in atorvastatin that react: carboxylic acid and amide.\nNew functional groups formed: (primary) alcohol and amine.
